turns.t: Mrs Whitcombe, good morning. I've got the letter here from your pharmacist, saying your pulse felt uneven when she checked it. Who've you brought with you?
This is Maria, she looks after me in the week. She's marvellous, she does the most wonderful soup, leek and potato, though I tell her not so much pepper.
Hello, doctor. I'm her carer, I live in at the moment. Mrs Whitcombe asked me to come in and help her remember things.
That's a good idea. Now, Mrs Whitcombe, what did you notice that made you go to the pharmacy in the first place?
Well, I was in for something else, really, I wanted a new hairbrush, the old one lost half its bristles, and she said would I like my pulse done.
Ah, so the pharmacist did it on her own initiative. And since then, have you felt anything yourself?
A fluttering, here in my chest, like a bird caught in a net. Comes and goes, been about two weeks.
A fluttering, on and off, for about two weeks. Anything else with it?
I get a bit light-headed if I stand up too fast, but I put that down to age.
She did go wobbly on Tuesday in the kitchen, doctor. She held on to the counter and it passed.
Thank you, Maria, that's helpful. Mrs Whitcombe, I need to ask you something that may seem to come out of nowhere. Do you have any allergies?
Allergies? Oh dear. I think I might be allergic to something, but I couldn't tell you what.
Go on, what makes you think so?
Years ago, something gave me a reaction. I can't remember the thing, or what it did. Perhaps it was a cream, or perhaps a tablet. Or the wallpaper paste, in the old house.
She's said that to me as well, doctor. A bad turn after something, but never a name.
So a possible allergy, no name, nothing known about what it did. We'll note it as uncertain and be careful. Maria, can you help us find out from her old records?
I'll ask her daughter. She keeps the folders.
Yes, Helen has everything in folders. Labelled, even. Colour coded.
Lovely. Now, let me do your observations. Arm out for me, please.
Blood pressure is 142/88. Pulse is 92, and it's irregular. Temperature is 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation is 97%.
Is that good? I never know which number matters.
Mostly fine. The irregular pulse is what I'd like to look at more closely. I'd like to do an ECG today, which is a tracing of the heart's rhythm.
Will it hurt? Is it the one with the sticky pads?
Sticky pads, yes, ten of them, but no pain. The nurse will do it before you leave.
I'll hold your handbag, Mrs Whitcombe.
Thank you, dear. Doctor, can I still have my evening sherry?
A small one is not a problem today. Tell me, how much do you drink, as a rule?
Oh, I like a drink of an evening, just a small sherry. The odd glass at Christmas, otherwise.
That's modest. Let's see what the tracing shows before I say more.
Of course. I don't want to make a fuss, I know you're busy.
Not at all. If the fluttering gets worse, or you feel faint or have chest pain, please ring us straight away.
I'll keep an eye on her and make a note of when it happens.
Maria writes everything in a little book. She's got me down as 'chatty'.
Accurate, I'd say. If the fluttering gets any worse, please ring us, and if you faint, call an ambulance.
Right. Thank you, doctor.
Mind how you go, both of you. The ECG room is on your left.
